nameStory: The 'cockspur' part of this tree's name comes from its long, sharp thorns that reminded early botanists of a rooster's fighting spurs. The 'broad-leaved' descriptor helps distinguish it from its close relative, the regular cockspur hawthorn, which has narrower leaves. Some folks also call it plumleaf hawthorn because its leaves have a similar shape to those of plum trees.
description: Broad-leaved cockspurthorn is a small to medium-sized tree in the rose family, typically growing 15-25 feet tall with a rounded, spreading crown. Like other hawthorns, it's armed with long, sharp thorns and produces clusters of white flowers in spring followed by small, apple-like fruits. This species is actually thought to be a natural hybrid between two other hawthorns, which explains its somewhat sporadic distribution in the wild. It's popular as an ornamental tree, especially in smaller gardens where its manageable size and attractive form make it a standout choice.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Broad, oval leaves with a leathery texture that are notably wider than most other hawthorns. They're dark green and glossy on top with shallow lobes or large teeth along the edges, feeling substantial and thick when you handle them.

idTips.label: Thorns
idTips.description: Long, straight, sharp thorns up to 3 inches long that emerge from the branches like deadly daggers. They're much longer and more prominent than on many other trees, making this species unmistakably armed and dangerous to handle carelessly.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Clusters of small white flowers with five petals each, appearing in flat-topped groups in late spring. The flowers have a sweet, somewhat musky fragrance and numerous pink-tipped stamens that give the flower clusters a slightly fuzzy appearance.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small, round, red to dark red fruits about the size of large peas that persist well into winter. They feel firm when ripe and have a dry, mealy texture with several hard seeds inside, making them look like tiny apples.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a dense, rounded crown with somewhat horizontal branching that creates an attractive, sculptural silhouette. The tree often has multiple trunks or low branching, giving it a shrub-like appearance when young.

habitat: This rare hawthorn is found in open woodlands, woodland edges, and occasionally in old fields or along fence rows where it has escaped cultivation. In New England, it's extremely uncommon in the wild, with only a few documented populations, though it may be found in parks and gardens as an ornamental tree. It prefers well-drained soils and full to partial sun.

seasonality.spring: White flower clusters appear in late spring after the leaves have emerged, creating a showy display. The broad leaves unfurl early and are initially pale green before darkening.
seasonality.summer: Leaves are at their glossiest dark green, and small green fruits begin developing. The thorns are most visible when the tree is in full leaf.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellow to orange-red before dropping, while the red fruits ripen and become more prominent. The fall color can be quite attractive but isn't always reliable.
seasonality.winter: The long, prominent thorns and persistent red fruits make identification possible even without leaves. The dense, thorny branching pattern and small red fruits clinging to bare branches are distinctive winter features.

funFact: This tree is essentially nature's own hybrid experiment - scientists believe it formed naturally when two different hawthorn species cross-pollinated, and now some populations can reproduce themselves from seed, essentially becoming a new species right before our eyes!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with cockspur hawthorn, its likely parent species, but broad-leaved cockspurthorn has noticeably wider, more substantial leaves. Remember: if the leaves look broad enough to remind you of plum tree leaves, you've probably found the broad-leaved species rather than the regular cockspur hawthorn with its narrower foliage.
contextualKnowledge: This species is so rare in New England that spotting one in the wild would be a significant find worth reporting to local botanists. Most specimens you'll encounter are likely planted ornamentals, particularly the popular 'Prunifolia' cultivar that's considered one of the best small trees for gardens.
compareHints: Among New England's many hawthorns, broad-leaved cockspurthorn stands out for its exceptionally broad, substantial leaves that are wider than most of its relatives. While dotted hawthorn and fleshy hawthorn (one of its supposed parents) also have broader leaves, neither has the same combination of very long thorns and the distinctive leaf shape that resembles plum leaves. The cockspur hawthorn, its other likely parent, has much narrower leaves and a more horizontal branching pattern.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Dotted hawthorn stands out from its many New England relatives primarily by its spotted fruits.
Among New England's many hawthorn species, common hawthorn stands out for having just one seed per fruit (most others have 2-5 seeds) and deeply lobed leaves with 3-7 divisions.
Among New England's many hawthorn species, cockspur stands out with the longest thorns - much longer than dotted hawthorn's short spines or Washington hawthorn's modest thorns.
Among New England's many hawthorn species, big-fruit hawthorn stands out for its notably larger berries and earlier bloom time.
Among New England hawthorns, large-thorn hawthorn stands out primarily for its exceptionally long, straight thorns that dwarf those of relatives like dotted hawthorn or common hawthorn.

Among the many hawthorn species in New England, Washington hawthorn stands out with its distinctly triangular, deeply lobed leaves (rather than the more oval or rounded leaves of species like dotted hawthorn).
Among New England's many hawthorn species, waxy-fruited hawthorn stands out primarily for its distinctively coated berries - no other local hawthorn has that waxy, frosted appearance on the fruits.

Among New England's many hawthorns, fireberry hawthorn stands out for its golden-yellow unripe fruits - most relatives like dotted hawthorn or cockspur hawthorn have green unripe fruits that turn red.
Large-flowered cockspurthorn stands out from its many hawthorn relatives primarily by its notably large flowers - nearly twice the size of most other hawthorns.
Among New England hawthorns, fanleaf hawthorn is distinguished by its broader, more fan-shaped leaves compared to most relatives.
Among New England hawthorns, Biltmore hawthorn stands out for its green, yellow, or orange fruits - most others like dotted hawthorn, common hawthorn, and cockspur hawthorn have red fruits.

Cleft-leaved hawthorn's leaves are much more deeply divided than most New England hawthorns - while dotted hawthorn has shallow lobes and cockspur hawthorn has barely any lobes at all, this species' leaves are cut nearly to the midrib.

Among New England's hawthorns, pea hawthorn stands out for having the smallest fruits in the genus - significantly smaller than the cherry-sized fruits of dotted hawthorn or the larger berries of cockspur hawthorn.
Among New England's many hawthorns, downy hawthorn stands out for its distinctly fuzzy leaf undersides - most others like dotted hawthorn or common hawthorn have smooth or only slightly hairy leaves.
Blanchard's hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having more deeply lobed leaves and longer thorns.
Miss Jones' hawthorn is distinguished from other New England hawthorns primarily by subtle differences in leaf shape, thorn characteristics, and fruit details that require close examination.
Stone's hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having more deeply lobed leaves and different fruit characteristics.
Fleshy hawthorn stands out from its many hawthorn relatives by having the juiciest, most succulent berries in the group.
Among New England's many hawthorn species, scarlet hawthorn is distinguished by its particularly prominent thorns and bright red fruits.
Among New England's many hawthorn species, Schuette's hawthorn is distinguished by subtle characteristics that require expert identification.
Northern hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having less deeply lobed leaves and different fruit characteristics, though these distinctions can be subtle.
Dodge's hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having less prominently marked leaves and typically fewer, larger thorns.
Holmes' hawthorn is most closely related to scarlet hawthorn but distinguished by its more elongated leaves and egg-shaped rather than round fruits.
Hairy cockspurthorn differs from its closest relative, downy hawthorn, primarily in having about 10 stamens per flower instead of 20, and the two species have separate native ranges.

Grove hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having longer thorns and less deeply cut leaves.
Keep's Hawthorn differs from common hawthorns like dotted hawthorn in subtle leaf lobe patterns and fruit characteristics that require expert knowledge to distinguish reliably.

Among New England hawthorns, poplar hawthorn stands out immediately for its broad, oval, relatively unlobed leaves - most other hawthorns like dotted hawthorn or common hawthorn have deeply cut, lobed leaves.
Unlike the common red-fruited hawthorns like dotted hawthorn or cockspur hawthorn, straw-fruited hawthorn produces distinctively pale yellow berries.

Among New England's many hawthorn species, stinking hawthorn stands out for its yellow-green fruits with red markings rather than the solid red fruits of most others like dotted hawthorn or cockspur hawthorn.
